items.prompt: What does calibration compare?
choices: Speed of answers and their accuracy
Stated confidence and hit rate
Facts known and facts forgotten
Effort spent and result achieved
items.explanation: Calibration lines up the number you state with how often calls at that number come true.

items.prompt: Can one prediction show whether someone is well-calibrated?
choices: No, it takes many calls at one level
Yes, if that call turned out to be right
Yes, if that call turned out to be wrong
Yes, if the person sounded very sure of it
items.explanation: A 90% call already admits a miss, so one result says almost nothing.

items.prompt: Rosa says "90%" on 200 mornings. About how many should bring rain if she is calibrated?
choices: About 100
About 120
About 200
About 180

items.prompt: What does Rosa do that Ben never does?
choices: Checks the sky again at noon before deciding
Reads a weather book before each forecast
Writes a percentage down before knowing
Asks a neighbor what they expect, then agrees
items.explanation: Her written number is what lets her check herself later.

items.prompt: Calibration is mainly about your...
choices: memory for the facts you know
confidence in your answers
speed of recall under pressure
years of experience in the field
items.explanation: It concerns how sure you say you are, not what you know.

items.prompt: Ben and Rosa have the same twenty years. What differs?
choices: Rosa checks her confidence against outcomes
Rosa lives in a rainier town than Ben ever did
Rosa knows far more weather terms than Ben does
Rosa has watched many more mornings than Ben
items.explanation: Experience was equal. The checking was not.

items.prompt: A forecaster says "80%." How often should the event fail if calibrated?
choices: About 1 time in 2
About 1 time in 10
Almost never
About 1 time in 5
items.explanation: 80% means about 20% misses.

items.prompt: Which statement is about calibration?
choices: I answered 70% of the exam questions correctly
I read 70% of the weather reports last year
When I say 70%, I am right 70% of the time
I finish 70% of my tasks within a minute
items.explanation: Only the first links a stated number to a hit rate.

items.prompt: Over a year, Rosa made 50 calls at "60%" and 50 calls at "90%." Which result would show she is well-calibrated?
choices: About 45 of the 60% calls and about 30 of the 90% calls came true
About 30 of the 60% calls and about 45 of the 90% calls came true
About 25 of the 60% calls and about 25 of the 90% calls came true
About 50 of the 60% calls and about 50 of the 90% calls came true
items.explanation: 60% of 50 is 30 and 90% of 50 is 45. Each bucket should match its own number.
items.reference:
Rosa vs. Ben at "90% sure" (assumed counts)
🌧️ Rosa: 178 of 200 rained, 89%
☁️ Ben: 116 of 200 rained, 58%
📏 Calibrated: hit rate matches the stated number
Why: calibration compares a stated confidence with the real hit rate across many calls, so a single result cannot settle it.
items.learnMore:
Calibration is a match between a number and a record

Saying 90% is a claim about a group of calls: about 9 in 10 should come true. It is checked across many calls, never by one result.

Common mistake

Judging a confidence level by whether the latest call came true.
items.reflection: Think of someone whose "definitely" you trust and someone whose "definitely" you discount. What record, if any, are you judging them by?

items.prompt: Two forecasters each say "90%" on 100 days. A is right on 90 days and B is right on 100. Who is better calibrated?
choices: A, because 90 hits matches the stated 90%
B, because 100 hits beats the stated 90%
Both equally, because both were right most days
Neither, because 100 days is too few to say
items.explanation: B did well but understated their certainty slightly. Calibration rewards the match, not the higher count.

His knowledge must be out of date, or simply wrong in places
Knowledge and calibration differ: he can know more and be worse
Calibration only matters for people who happen to know little
items.explanation: Calibration concerns confidence, so a knowledgeable person can still state numbers that do not match their record.

items.prompt: Someone says 90% and lands 58%. What is this pattern?
choices: Underconfidence
Overconfidence
Good calibration
Pure bad luck
items.explanation: The stated number is far above the real hit rate.

items.prompt: Someone says 60% and lands 90%. What is this pattern?
choices: Underconfidence
Overconfidence
Good calibration
Pure good luck
items.explanation: The stated number is far below the real hit rate.

items.prompt: A calibrated forecaster who says 80% should be wrong how often?
choices: Never
About 1 call in 2
About 4 calls in 5
About 1 call in 5
items.explanation: 20% misses are exactly what 80% promises.

items.prompt: Which sounds like an overconfident engineer?
choices: Says "maybe 60%" about things that nearly always work
Says "I will check the log first" before changes
Says "95% sure, ship it" and is often surprised
Says "I never estimate" about anything unsure
items.explanation: Certainty that outruns the record is overconfidence.

items.prompt: Which sounds like an underconfident engineer?
choices: Says "95% sure, ship it" and is often surprised by it
Hedges at "maybe 60%" on calls right 90% of the time
Says "definitely" and is right every single time they say it
Says "no idea" about calls they have never made before
items.explanation: Their record is better than their numbers admit.

items.prompt: Is "always right" the goal of calibration?
choices: No, matching confidence to hit rate is
Yes, it is the whole point of the exercise
Yes, whenever the stakes are high enough
No, being wrong as often as possible is
items.explanation: A calibrated 80% is meant to miss about 1 in 5.

items.prompt: Overconfidence mainly harms others by...
choices: Making every call come out wrong
Slowing down every decision that is made
Hiding the real skill of the person
Being trusted at a number too high
items.explanation: People act on the number, and the number overstated the odds.

items.prompt: Underconfidence's main cost is...
choices: Too many wrong calls get shipped
Frequent surprises when things fail
Real skill gets discounted or ignored
A hit rate that looks suspiciously perfect
items.explanation: Listeners cannot hear the signal under the hedging.

items.prompt: A says "95%" and is right 70% of the time. B says "55%" and is right 55%. C says "60%" and is right 90%. Which set of labels is correct?
choices: A underconfident, B well-calibrated, C overconfident
A overconfident, B well-calibrated, C underconfident
A overconfident, B underconfident, C well-calibrated
A well-calibrated, B overconfident, C underconfident
items.explanation: A states more than the record supports, B matches, and C states less than the record supports.
items.reference:
Two opposite misses
🔥 Over: says 90%, lands 58% (Ben)
🧊 Under: says 60%, lands 90%
✅ Well-calibrated: says 90%, lands 89% (Rosa)
Why: overconfidence and underconfidence are opposite errors, and neither is the same as being right or wrong more often.
items.learnMore:
Too high and too low are both misses

Overconfident people get trusted for numbers they have not earned. Underconfident people hide real skill behind hedges. A calibrated person misses exactly as often as their number says.

Common mistake

Treating "always right" as the goal, so a calibrated 80% looks like a failure.
items.reflection: Do you tend to say "definitely" or "maybe" more than your record deserves? Where would you look to find out?

items.prompt: Someone is right on 99 of 100 calls they each labeled "90%." Which description fits best?
choices: Mildly underconfident: 90% was a bit low for them
Badly overconfident, because 99 is too high to be real
Perfectly calibrated, because they were mostly right
Overconfident, because they were right more than expected
items.explanation: Being right more than the label says means the label was too low.

items.prompt: To check a stated confidence, you first...
choices: Average every call into a single number
Bucket calls by stated confidence
Throw away the calls that missed
Wait for one decisive call
items.explanation: Each stated level has its own hit rate to check.

items.prompt: What is a "bucket" in a track record?
choices: Calls at the same stated confidence
All of the calls made on the same day
All calls that turned out to be right
All calls made on the same topic
items.explanation: Buckets are defined by the stated number.

items.prompt: Out of 10 calls at 80%, the most likely result is...
choices: 10 hits
6 hits
5 hits
8 hits
items.explanation: Eight hits has the highest chance, about 30%.

items.prompt: Is 6 hits out of 10 at 80% strong evidence of overconfidence?
choices: Yes, one small bucket is always conclusive
Yes, any single miss at all proves it
No, a calibrated person gets this often
No, misses never count against you
items.explanation: Six or fewer happens about 12% of the time to a calibrated person.

items.prompt: More calls in a bucket make the hit rate...
choices: Harder to compare with the stated number
A steadier guide to the real hit rate
Irrelevant to calibration
Always closer to 100%
items.explanation: Larger samples bounce around less.

items.prompt: On the chart, a perfectly calibrated forecaster's bars...
choices: Match the stated number at every level
Sit at 100 for every stated level
Sit below the stated level each time
Are all equal to each other at every level
items.explanation: 60% bar at 60, 75% bar at 75, 90% bar at 90.

items.prompt: Ben's shortfall is largest at which stated level?
choices: They are the same size
items.explanation: His gaps are 5, 11 and 32 points.

items.prompt: Someone says 70% on 100 calls and is right on 95. Pattern?
choices: Overconfident
Well-calibrated
Underconfident
Cannot be told
items.explanation: Their number is far below their hit rate.

items.prompt: One person labels 10 calls "80%" and hits 6. Another labels 100 calls "80%" and hits 65. Which reading is best supported?
choices: The first shows it more, since 6 of 10 is nearer a coin flip
The second shows overconfidence far more convincingly
Both show it about equally, since both land below 80%
Neither shows it, since both hit more than half the time
items.explanation: 6 or fewer of 10 happens to a calibrated person about 12% of the time. 65 or fewer of 100 happens about 0.03% of the time.
items.reference:
10 calls at a true 80% (chance of each result)
8 hits: 30.2%, the single most likely result
6 or fewer hits: about 12%
65 or fewer of 100 hits: about 0.03%
Why: small buckets bounce around the true rate, so only large buckets can convict a stated number.
items.learnMore:
Bucket by confidence, then ask how many calls

Sort calls by the number you stated, check the hit rate in each bucket, and ask how likely that result would be for someone calibrated exactly. A short run of misses is common. A long one is not.

Common mistake

Reading 6 of 10 at 80% as proof of overconfidence.

items.prompt: What are the four steps, in order?
choices: Observe, predict, adjust, compare
Predict, observe, compare, adjust
Compare, predict, observe, adjust
Adjust, observe, predict, compare
items.explanation: You commit first, then learn the result, then check, then change.

items.prompt: What does "predict" require?
choices: A number written before the outcome
A vague guess such as probably
A decision made after the outcome
A long written explanation of reasons
items.explanation: A number you can be scored against is what makes the rest possible.

items.prompt: What is the compare step?
choices: Checking a single call against its own result
Checking your own memory against a friend's
Checking this year's result against last year's
Checking many same-level calls against hit rate
items.explanation: Comparison needs a record of many calls.

items.prompt: Why does Ben not improve?
choices: He has too few mornings of experience
He does not look at the sky
He never records a number to check
He guesses less often than Rosa does
items.explanation: Without a recorded number there is nothing to compare.

items.prompt: What does "adjust" mean?
choices: Raising every number you ever state
Changing what a level means to you
Predicting only safe things
Dropping the misses from the log
items.explanation: If your 90% lands 60%, your 90% means about 60% for you.

items.prompt: Which builds calibration better?
choices: 50 predictions run through the full loop
500 predictions never written down
500 predictions remembered later
50 predictions made after the outcome
items.explanation: Loop quality beats raw volume.

items.prompt: Which step does editing your memory of what you predicted damage?
choices: Predict
Adjust
None of them
Observe
items.explanation: You stop seeing what actually happened relative to what you said.

items.prompt: A written record is needed because...
choices: Memory is perfect but takes a while
Numbers look more official on paper
One call never reveals calibration
Teams will always ask to see it
items.explanation: Only a pile of calls at one level can be compared.

items.prompt: After a deploy goes well, a lead says "I always knew it would be fine." Which step is being undermined?
choices: Adjust: she is changing her stated number much too quickly
Observe: with no written number, memory rewrites the past
Compare: she compared far too many separate calls at once
Predict: she predicted far too often to keep proper track
items.explanation: Without a written number, hindsight can claim any prediction after the fact.
items.reference:
The loop
1️⃣ Predict: a number, written before
2️⃣ Observe: the real outcome, unedited
3️⃣ Compare: many calls at one level
4️⃣ Adjust: change what the number means to you
Why: experience only becomes calibration when each stated number is checked against what happened.
items.learnMore:
Doing the task is not the same as running the loop

Volume of experience grows on its own. Feedback about your confidence only appears when a number was written first and compared later.

Common mistake

Assuming years on the job automatically calibrate you.
items.reflection: Pick a judgment you make often at work or at home. What would the first written "before" number look like?

Both equally, since each of them made 200 separate estimates
Neither, since 200 estimates is far too few to learn anything from
items.explanation: Equal volume, but only one of them ever received feedback on their confidence.

items.prompt: In Tomás's log, what changed over four months?
choices: His tasks became far easier to do
His "80%" calls came near 80%
He made far fewer estimates overall
He stopped writing any numbers down
items.explanation: The tasks stayed the same. His numbers started to match his record.

items.prompt: What must each log entry contain?
choices: A number before and a result after
A paragraph explaining the reasoning
A rating of how hard it all felt
A signed note from a teammate
items.explanation: Those two items are what make comparison possible.

items.prompt: What was Tomás's month 1 hit rate on "80%" calls?
items.explanation: Three of six hit.

items.prompt: Month 1 had 3 hits out of 6 at "80%." What was the gap from 80?
choices: 20 points
50 points
30 points
3 points
items.explanation: 80 minus 50 is 30.

items.prompt: May one log mix estimates and debugging hypotheses?
choices: No, each kind needs its own log
Yes, more entries show gaps sooner
No, hypotheses cannot carry numbers
Yes, but only if numbers are hidden
items.explanation: Calibration transfers across related calls, and more entries speed learning.

items.prompt: Month 4 had only 5 calls. How far does one miss move the hit rate?
choices: 20 points
5 points
1 point
50 points
items.explanation: One call is 1 of 5, which is 20%.

items.prompt: Did Tomás's tasks get easier?
choices: Yes, he chose simpler tasks
Yes, the team assigned easier ones
No, they became far harder
No, what changed was his feedback
items.explanation: He got feedback on his confidence for the first time.

items.prompt: What does a log give that a gut feeling does not?
choices: A much stronger feeling of certainty
A guarantee that you will be right often
An outside record to check against
A shortcut that skips doing the task
items.explanation: The record can disagree with the feeling.

items.prompt: One month has 4 "80%" calls with 2 hits. Another has 40 calls with 20 hits. What do they say?
choices: The 4-call month is stronger because it is easier to read
Both are 50%, but the 40-call month is far stronger evidence
Only the 40-call month has a rate, because 4 is too few
Both are equally strong because the rates are equal
items.explanation: A small bucket is compatible with a calibrated person fairly often. Twenty of 40 would be very unlikely at a true 80%.
items.reference:
Tomás's "80%" calls (assumed counts)
Month 1: 3 of 6, gap 30
Month 2: 4 of 7, gap 23
Month 3: 4 of 6, gap 13
Month 4: 4 of 5, gap 0 (but only 5 calls)
Why: a log turns a vague sense of certainty into a record, and a small month is a noisy part of it.
items.learnMore:
A log is feedback your gut never had

Each entry needs a number before and a checkable result after. Trends over months matter more than any single month, because a few calls swing the rate widely.

Common mistake

Reading one small month as proof of mastery or of failure.

choices: Five calls is too few; one miss would move the rate by 20 points
True, since a gap of 0 means nothing is left to learn
False, since a gap below 5 points is only rounding
True, but only if month 5 also reaches a gap of 0
items.explanation: The trend is encouraging, but a month of 5 calls cannot establish perfection.
items.reference:
Tomás's "80%" calls (assumed counts)
Month 1: 3 of 6, gap 30
Month 2: 4 of 7, gap 23
Month 3: 4 of 6, gap 13
Month 4: 4 of 5, gap 0 (but only 5 calls)
Why: a log turns a vague sense of certainty into a record, and a small month is a noisy part of it.
items.learnMore:
A log is feedback your gut never had

Each entry needs a number before and a checkable result after. Trends over months matter more than any single month, because a few calls swing the rate widely.

Common mistake

Reading one small month as proof of mastery or of failure.

Proof he stopped logging honestly
Plausible noise: months of 5 to 7 calls bounce around a smooth trend
items.explanation: A 3-point difference on 6 calls is under one call's worth of swing.

It understates his reliability, since it skips risky calls
It overstates how reliable his numbers are, since the misses are the evidence
It is unaffected, since the numbers were written beforehand
items.explanation: Choosing entries afterward breaks the "before" discipline and hides exactly what the log should show.

items.prompt: What share of Tomás's "95%" calls hit?
items.explanation: Thirteen of 20 landed.

items.prompt: Which level of his scale ran hottest relative to its record?
items.explanation: It stated 95 and delivered 65.

items.prompt: How many "95%" calls would you expect to miss out of 20?
choices: About 7
About 10
About 19
About 1
items.explanation: 5% of 20 is 1.

items.prompt: What did the log give that "be more careful" does not?
choices: A cure for every kind of mistake
A reason to estimate much less
A specific level to fix
A way to skip reviews
items.explanation: It names which level is unreliable.

items.prompt: What is Tomás's new rule for his own "95%"?
choices: Never state a number above 80%
A second reviewer before acting
Always state 95% so it feels right
Act on it twice as quickly
items.explanation: His "95%" has not earned the trust it asks for.

items.prompt: Tomás's "70%" calls were...
choices: Close to accurate all along
Far too high for what he said
Far too low to be useful
Never recorded in the log at all
items.explanation: He could trust that part of his scale more.

items.prompt: "Be more careful" is best described as...
choices: A precise diagnosis of the problem
A calibration measure for a level
A log entry for the week
Untargeted: no level named
items.explanation: It gives no way to tell which calls need work.

items.prompt: What caused the outage?
choices: A task he had never done before in his role
An unlogged "70%" call made earlier that week
A "95% safe" call that was far less safe
A reviewer who disagreed with his plan
items.explanation: The timeout bump interacted with a retry storm nobody had modeled, and the 95% label hid that.

items.prompt: Tomás's "95%" calls hit 65% of 20, and his "70%" calls hit 70%. Which response matches the data?
choices: Distrust all of his labels equally until further notice
Distrust his "95%" label only; keep trusting "70%"
Trust his "95%" label and distrust his "70%" label
Lower every label he uses by exactly 30 points
items.explanation: Only the top of his scale ran hot, so the fix should be limited to it.
items.reference:
Tomás's scale (assumed counts)
🚨 "95%" calls: 13 of 20 hit, 65%
⚠️ "80%" calls: 30 points high in month 1
✅ "70%" calls: close to accurate
🔧 Fix: get a reviewer on any "95%" call
Why: a log can show which part of your scale runs hot, which a general resolution to be careful cannot.
items.learnMore:
Find the level that is wrong, then fix only that

A record can show that one stretch of your confidence scale is badly off while others are fine. A targeted rule fixes that stretch without damaging the rest.

Common mistake

Responding to a mistake with general caution, which spreads doubt over calls that were sound.
items.reflection: Think of a mistake that taught you to "be more careful." What was the specific thing that was actually off?

items.prompt: Why is 7 misses in 20 at a stated 95% a pattern rather than bad luck?
choices: Calibrated 95% people see this about 1 time in 30,000
Seven is more than a third of the twenty calls made
Twenty calls is always enough to be completely certain
Any single miss at a stated 95% proves overconfidence
items.explanation: Expected misses are about 1, and 7 or more has a probability near 0.003%.

items.prompt: Why are two-year architecture bets hard to calibrate on?
choices: They cannot be given a number at all
They resolve rarely and murkily
They always turn out to be right
They need a bigger team to check
items.explanation: Few cycles and tangled causes both work against the loop.

items.prompt: A proxy prediction is...
choices: A quicker test of the same judgment
A prediction made by someone else
A guess with no number attached to it
A prediction that never resolves at all
items.explanation: It is a stand-in that can actually be checked soon.

items.prompt: About how many resolved predictions per year does a two-year bet give?
choices: About 13
About 1.5
About 24
About 0.5
items.explanation: One resolution per two years is 0.5 per year.

items.prompt: A proxy that resolves every 4 weeks gives how many per year?
items.explanation: 52 weeks divided by 4 is 13.

items.prompt: Why is a slow outcome "noisy"?
choices: It was measured with a badly faulty tool
Other changes along the way muddy it
It was easy to remember afterward
It always matches the prediction
items.explanation: Team changes and shifting requirements mix into the result.

items.prompt: Which is a fast proxy for "this design is easy to extend"?
choices: "75% sure the interface changes in two features"
"I have a good feeling about this design overall"
"The whole team likes the architecture diagram"
"We will simply wait and see in two years"
items.explanation: It carries a number and resolves in weeks.

items.prompt: A fair proxy must...
choices: Be easier to guess correctly each time
Have nothing to do with the bet at hand
Resolve only after a year or more
Shake your belief if it fails
items.explanation: Otherwise you are calibrating a different judgment.

items.prompt: For slow bets, calibration is...
choices: Impossible in any form at all
Unneeded for the really important calls
Possible mainly with faster stand-ins
Automatic after enough experience
items.explanation: Proxies create enough cycles to learn from.

items.prompt: Which proxy best stands in for "this new hire will still be a strong fit in two years"?
choices: "70% sure the rest of the team will enjoy lunch with them soon"
"70% sure their first owned project ships cleanly in 8 weeks"
"70% sure they will accept the offer we have made them"
"70% sure they will still be at the company a year from now"
items.explanation: It resolves soon and is about the same underlying judgment, how well they will perform on real work.
items.reference:
Resolved predictions per year (assumed timings)
🐢 Two-year architecture bet: 0.5 per year
⚡ Proxy resolving every 4 weeks: 13 per year
⚖️ A proxy is fair only if missing it would shake the original belief
Why: slow, tangled outcomes give too few clean cycles, so you calibrate on faster stand-ins that test the same judgment.
items.learnMore:
Manufacture faster cycles for slow bets

Feedback can be rare and also confounded by team changes and new requirements. Fast, clean proxy predictions that test the same judgment give many more checks.

Common mistake

Choosing a proxy that is easy to resolve but unrelated to the original judgment.
items.reflection: Name a decision you are waiting on that will not resolve for months. What smaller prediction about it could resolve in weeks?

About 52, roughly 100 times as many
items.explanation: 52 divided by 6 is about 8.7, which is about 17 times 0.5.
